analysis.one_liner: Bars drug makers from owning pharmacy benefit managers and forces PBMs to disclose payments and drug-switch savings.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House committee with only 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that employers and insurers hire to run prescription drug benefits. This bill would have forbidden drug manufacturers from owning PBMs, banned PBMs from switching patients to more expensive drugs without telling them the savings, and required PBMs to disclose every payment they receive from drug makers to their clients and to the Justice Department. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee in May 2005, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with prescription drug coverage, who would learn when a PBM switches their drug and whether the switch saves them money. Employers, unions, and insurers that hire PBMs would see the full picture of PBM income from drug makers, letting them negotiate lower drug costs. Independent pharmacies and generic drug makers would also benefit from limits on switching away from generics.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with drug coverage and their employers

how_it_helps.text: PBMs would be barred from proposing a drug switch that raises the net cost of the prescription [S3].
PBMs could not switch a patient from a drug with generic equivalents to a brand-name drug without generics unless the switch cost less than every generic alternative [S3].
PBMs would have to tell each patient, clearly and conspicuously, the savings from any drug switch [S3].

Every quarter, PBMs would have to disclose to their client plans and to the Justice Department's Antitrust Division all money received from drug manufacturers — including market-share incentives, commissions, mail-service discounts, and administrative fees [S3].
PBMs would have to reveal, before a client signs a contract, how they solicit and receive payments from drug manufacturers, and drug makers could no longer hold a controlling interest in a PBM [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers, whose secret rebate and fee income from drug manufacturers would become public and whose drug-switching practices would be restricted. Brand-name drug manufacturers, which could no longer own PBMs and whose payments to PBMs would be disclosed. Violations involving federal payment claims could bring False Claims Act liability, multiplying the financial exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and brand-name drug makers

drawbacks.text: Transparency rules add paperwork costs for PBMs and drug makers, and critics of such rules argue those costs can be passed on to plans and consumers; the bill also relies on the Health and Human Services Secretary to set penalties, leaving enforcement strength uncertain [S2].

Disclosure alone does not directly cap drug prices; consumers would benefit mainly through better-informed employers and plans negotiating on their behalf, and the bill does nothing for people without drug coverage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: shining light on PBM-manufacturer payments and blocking self-serving drug switches would give employers and consumers leverage they currently lack, at the cost of compliance paperwork and heavier federal enforcement. The design is narrow — it regulates conduct and disclosure rather than capping prices — so its impact depends on plans actually using the disclosed information to bargain harder.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee from April 2005 until Congress ended in January 2007, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Anthony Weiner of New York introduced the Pharmacy Benefit Manager Transparency Act of 2005 on April 14, 2005, joined by Rep. Moran of Kansas [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S1].
On May 13, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill attracted only 2 cosponsors, both Republicans [S4].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill received no vote in the House or Senate [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and brand-name drug makers are better off: the secrecy around PBM payments from drug makers and drug switches remained untouched, and no competing transparency bill advanced either. The 2-cosponsor support level suggests the bill never had a realistic path regardless.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and brand-name drug makers

for.name: Rep. Anthony D. Weiner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to committee

for.name: Rep. Jerry Moran of Kansas
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's Republican cosponsor at introduction

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; neither the committee nor its Health Subcommittee held a hearing or markup, and the bill was never reported out

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democratic sponsor and 2 Republican cosponsors — but with only 3 supporters total it never reached a vote, so no recorded partisan split exists.

industries.note: PBMs profit from rebate and fee arrangements with drug makers and from drug-switching practices that the bill would force into the open. Their business model depends on intermediation that clients cannot fully see; the bill would expose that income each quarter to clients and the Justice Department.

Drug makers would be barred from owning PBMs — cutting off a channel to influence which drugs patients get — and their payments to PBMs would be disclosed. The bill targets manufacturer-PBM deals precisely because they can steer patients to higher-cost brand drugs.

industries.industry: Employers, unions, and health plans that hire PBMs
industries.note: These client plans would finally see what their PBM earns from drug manufacturers, giving them leverage to negotiate lower drug costs for their members. Their interest runs alongside consumers' interests here.

industries.industry: Generic drug makers and independent pharmacies
industries.note: Rules against switching patients away from drugs with generic equivalents would preserve generic prescriptions, benefiting generic manufacturers and the pharmacies that dispense them.
